title: Is there an anti-AI supermajority?
subtitle: Still Counting EP2 is out.
contentHtml:
This has been one of those weeks when it feels like everything Silver Bulletin covers is happening at once. Democrats have continued to have a very good run of polling since Labor Day, with our Senate forecast ever-so-slightly breaking out of “toss-up” range into “Lean D”. And the AI and political worlds are colliding in their sharpest way since the battle between Anthropic and the Department of Defense in February.

Meanwhile, in less existential and more fun territory for our sports readers, our first ELWAY and QBERT updates of the season are ready. These models develop fairly aggressive opinions even early in the season. We’ve made more of our QBERT data free — more on that down below.

But let’s get back to politics. Our second official episode of Still Counting is ready for your viewing and/or listening pleasure. And it’s a highly topical one. We discussed Democrats’ recent gains in midterm election polls. The rest of the episode focuses on the rapidly developing politics of AI:

We think it makes sense for the time being to send these episodes out every week, typically on Wednesday evening or Thursday morning. While Silver Bulletin and Still Counting have no formal affiliation, the metrics from previous posts suggest the audiences are overlapping enough that this is probably a win-win.

Most weeks, we’ll also try to include a little bonus content in the post: additional context about the episode, Silver Bulletin site news/announcements/coming attractions, or both. (We’re reserving the right to skip all of this when things get really busy.)

This does mean roughly one extra email from us every week, but there’s a convenient workaround if you’re not interested in the Still Counting post. See the bottom of today’s newsletter if you don’t want to receive the Still Counting email.

The context: An emerging supermajority for AI regulation

It’s not your imagination: suddenly everybody is talking about AI. AI has been our semi-official third beat at Silver Bulletin (along with politics and sports) and I’ll admit it’s interesting to see some of the topics we’ve been talking about for years suddenly go mainstream.

But first contact between the AI safety community and normie politics was always going to be an important moment — and a weird one, considering how eccentric people in the broader AI/effective altruist/rationalist community tend to be. (I say that mostly in a loving/respectful way. For a thorough taxonomy of all of these groups and how EAs came to dominate AI, see my book.)

It’s been widely predicted that AI would devolve into a highly partisan issue once it hit the mainstream. There’s certainly been a lot of vitriol on Twitter. But that conspicuously hasn’t been true in the polling so far.

Take this fresh polling from Politico, for example:

Among Americans overall, 63 percent say there’s at least a “moderate risk” of AI destroying humanity, versus just 22 percent who assign “no risk” or a “very small risk”. And the splits among Trump and Harris voters are 61-29 and 70-21 respectively. So a slight gap if you squint, but a much narrower one than on almost any other contemporary issue.

The splits in a YouGov poll on the pace of AI advancement are similar:

Two-thirds of Americans think AI is advancing too quickly; only 2 percent say it’s too slow. Democrats are slightly more likely to say “too quickly”, but this position holds a supermajority among Republican voters also.

And of course, we’ve seen similar numbers on data centers also, as I discussed last month with Jasmine Sun.

Why — for now — is there such an apparent consensus? Well, there are a lot of concerns that voters might have about AI. In no particular order:

  • Taking jobs

  • Disempowering humanity or democracy

  • Existential risks

  • Impact on the educational system

  • Concerns about algorithmic or political bias — you can find plenty of people who think AI is “too woke” and others who say it’s not woke enough

  • Religious objections, as Clare talked about on the show

  • Environmental impacts

  • NIMBYism about data centers

  • Distrust of Big Tech

  • Concerns about wealth and power inequality

  • Cybersecurity or national security risks

  • Stealing intellectual property

  • And general apprehension about rapid change.

I don’t want to weigh in on which of these concerns I personally regard as being the most valid because I’m just one voter. I will say though that even as someone who is usually quite pro-growth/pro-technology, I have a lot of apprehension about the pace of change that AI leaders are talking about.

What’s working against that?

  • General pro-growth sentiment

  • Concerns about China lapping us

  • For some voters, perhaps extreme loyalty or trust in President Trump

  • Plus, people might personally find AI useful. They're certainly extremely popular consumer products.1

And then there’s a weird faction of AI denialists — people ostensibly on the left — who are convinced that AI is all a scam and therefore there isn’t much need for regulation. Maybe I’ll write about them some other time. But this isn’t anything approaching a mainstream position.2Bernie Sanders is in the “concerned” camp, as is Elizabeth Warren. (And so is Steve Bannon!)

So I don’t expect this pro-AI coalition to be very durable. The AI denialists and the Trump fans hate one another. Silicon Valley’s relationship with Trump spiraled into a mess last year. And for now, concern about China is pretty modest as compared to, say, the rivalry with the Soviet Union during the Cold War (or antipathy toward the “Axis of Evil” following 9/11).

It’s very hard to pass legislation through a polarized Congress, and it might get harder if FLIPR is right and Democrats win one or both chambers in November. But we don’t see this kind of bipartisan consensus all that often. I don’t know what odds I’d give, but I’m probably bullish on the odds of substantive regulation passing relative to the conventional wisdom.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • I know we’ve been heavy on paid content lately, so we’ve decided to move some of the cooler QBERT features in front of the paywall. All of the historical data is now free, including the interactive that allows you to compare the career trajectories of any quarterbacks since 1950. (The predictive components of QBERT and the depth charts will remain exclusive for paid subscribers, as will most of ELWAY.)

  • Believe it or not, we’re finally pulling out of a months-long hole after publishing the World Cup, midterms and NFL models basically back-to-back-to-back. So we hope to unpause SBSQ soon. We’ll also have the “summer” edition of our NBA Future of the Franchise rankings ready in the next week or two.

  • I was in the New York Times this week with 5 other polling experts. Based on FLIPR, it looks like I’m the most bullish on Democratic gains in the House.

How to unsubscribe from the weekly Still Counting post

It’s simple. Visit your Silver Bulletin account here or navigate to this URL: https://www.natesilver.net/account. You can then use the “Notifications” tab to turn emails from a particular section on and off.

FYI, we’d strongly recommend against turning “Models & Forecasts” off. These are only new model launches — so probably 3-4-ish posts per year — and not all Model Talks or related content. And there are some posts that don’t fit conveniently into any of these categories; before long, we may be writing about AI enough that it will need its own section.
